nameStory: The compass plant earned its name from a remarkable natural navigation trick - its leaves tend to align themselves north-south to avoid the harsh midday sun. This orientation was so reliable that prairie travelers and Native Americans used it as a living compass to find their way across vast grasslands.
description: Compass plant is a tall, prairie sunflower that can tower up to 8 feet high, making it one of the giants of the grassland. It produces bright yellow daisy-like flowers clustered at the top of sturdy stems from mid to late summer. The deeply cut, lobed leaves are distinctive and quite large, giving the plant a bold, architectural presence. Though native to prairie regions further west, it's extremely rare in New England with only a few recorded sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, deeply divided leaves with sharp, pointed lobes that feel rough and sandpapery to the touch. The leaves have a distinctive compass-like orientation, often aligning north-south.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers about 3-4 inches across with numerous thin petals radiating from a darker yellow center, clustered at the top of tall stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely tall plant reaching 6-8 feet in height with thick, sturdy stems that feel rigid and substantial when touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: When crushed, leaves and stems release a resinous, turpentine-like smell that's quite distinctive and somewhat medicinal.

habitat: In its native range, compass plant thrives in tall-grass prairies and open grasslands with deep, rich soils. Any New England sightings would likely be in cultivated prairie gardens, botanical collections, or restoration plantings rather than wild populations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as rosettes of deeply cut leaves close to the ground, already showing their characteristic rough texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification season with tall flowering stems and bright yellow blooms from July through August, plus the distinctive leaf orientation.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads develop, while leaves may show yellowing before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies completely back to ground level, leaving no above-ground traces until spring emergence.

funFact: Compass plant can live for over 100 years and develops a taproot that can plunge 15 feet deep into the soil - deeper than many trees - making it incredibly drought-resistant and nearly impossible to transplant once established.
confusionNotes: The deeply lobed leaves and tall stature make compass plant quite distinctive, but it could be confused with other tall sunflowers. Look for the characteristic sandpapery leaf texture and north-south leaf orientation that other sunflowers don't show.
contextualKnowledge: Compass plant is sometimes called 'pilotweed' or 'polarplant' for the same navigational reasons as its main common name. The resinous sap gives it another nickname - 'turpentine plant' - and was traditionally chewed like gum by Native Americans.
compareHints: Compass plant is much taller and has more deeply divided leaves than its relative cup plant, which has leaves that clasp around the stem forming little cups. Unlike starry rosinweed with its smaller flowers, compass plant produces large, showy blooms and grows to impressive heights that make it unmistakable among the rosinweeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cup plant is the only rosinweed (Silphium) species commonly found in New England, making it unique in the region.
Unlike its relatives cup plant and compass plant, starry rosinweed is much shorter and has smaller, rougher leaves that don't form distinctive cups around the stem.
